claim: Provenance can serve as an operational control signal in shared multi-agent memory, so that permission-ineligible, untrusted, or revoked sources are excluded and risky actions are gated before execution rather than only audited afterward.
method: MAP-Graph represents agents, sources, memories, claims, and actions in a typed execution graph, traces ancestry, excludes permission-ineligible records, reranks eligible memories by semantic similarity times multiplicative path trust, and applies a risk-sensitive gate before action execution while retaining affected lineage for audit.
evidence: Controlled benchmark of 2,700 synthetic tasks per method across three domains: 94.96% overall task success, 72.70% exact decision accuracy, 90.22% in the clean setting (success requires a correct Allow rather than a safe intervention); ablations isolate permission filtering, path trust, and action gating; transfer tests with two additional backbones preserve the exact-decision and access-control advantages.
stated_limitations: Results support provenance as an operational control signal 'within the evaluated setting'; otherwise not stated.
not_tested: Evaluation is on synthetic tasks only, with no real multi-agent workflows or naturally arising conflicts between writers; no measurement of whether trust-weighted reranking changes downstream task performance relative to a plain semantic retriever on non-adversarial content, and no report of collection or inference cost.
title: MAP-Graph: Provenance-Aware Shared Memory for Multi-Agent Workflows

claim: Agent memory, skills, and rules are points on a single axis of increasing experience compression, existing systems each operate at one fixed compression level (the 'missing diagonal'), and transferability rises with compression at the cost of specificity.
method: A survey and conceptual framework: citation analysis of 1,136 references across 22 primary papers, mapping of 20+ systems onto the Experience Compression Spectrum (5-20x episodic memory, 50-500x procedural skills, 1,000x+ declarative rules), and articulation of open problems and design principles.
evidence: Literature analysis only: cross-community citation rate below 1% between memory and skill-discovery communities; compression ratios and the 'missing diagonal' are derived from mapping published systems, with no new experiments reported in the abstract.
not_tested: No empirical experiment verifies that transferability actually increases with compression or that adaptive cross-level compression helps; the claimed compression ratios and their effect on latency and compute are not measured under matched conditions.
title: Experience Compression Spectrum: Unifying Memory, Skills, and Rules in LLM Agents

claim: A unified memory pool drawn from heterogeneous coding domains improves coding-agent performance, chiefly by transferring meta-knowledge such as validation routines, and abstraction level dictates transferability: high-level insights transfer while low-level traces can cause negative transfer.
method: Memory Transfer Learning: build a cross-domain memory pool and evaluate four memory representations ranging from concrete traces to abstract insights across coding benchmarks, varying pool size and the producing versus consuming model.
evidence: 6 coding benchmarks, four memory representations; cross-domain memory improves average performance by 3.7%; transfer effectiveness scales with memory pool size; memory can be transferred between different models.
not_tested: The abstract gives no detail on which model pairs were tested for cross-model transfer or how much of the writer's gain the reader keeps; no comparison against a same-cost self-collected pool, no seed or noise reporting, and no analysis of whether the reader can detect the harmful low-level traces.
title: Memory Transfer Learning: How Memories are Transferred Across Domains in Coding Agents

claim: Verbatim replay of retrieved experience causes negative transfer, and agents that critique and reconstruct retrieved experience conditioned on the current state outperform pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, especially out of distribution.
method: MemHarness: at each decision step a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting; the reconstructive ability is trained end-to-end with GRPO.
evidence: ALFWorld and WebShop; substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, with strong robustness in OOD scenarios; analyses indicate the reconstruction objective prevents negative transfer and acts as latent guidance during training (no numbers given in the abstract).
not_tested: Whether reconstruction still helps when the retrieved experience was written by a different or weaker model rather than the agent's own; how much of the gain comes from the RL training itself versus the reconstruction step at inference; per-step inference token cost of reconstructing at every decision.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed

claim: Governing an on-device agent's experience memory by a single net-value-per-byte score (value minus harm, per byte) reduces footprint, energy, uplink, and injection success together without reducing accuracy, so forgetting by net value improves the agent.
method: A score that drives three decisions: KEEP evicts low-value bytes under RAM and energy budgets, SHARE sends an insight to peers only when its value exceeds its uplink cost, and TRUST gates a peer entry by provenance.
evidence: Language-model-agent task-drift benchmarks and a heterogeneous Jetson testbed with two robot-arm nodes and a hub; memory reduced 2.7x, uplink 2.4x, injection success driven from 0.75 to zero, and higher accuracy on cases corrupted by poison or stale memory.
stated_limitations: 'In this setting, forgetting by net value improves the agent rather than weakening it'; otherwise not stated.
not_tested: How the value and harm terms are estimated and whether they hold beyond the small testbed; whether provenance-gated peer entries from a more capable or differently configured node still transfer useful content or are simply blocked; no comparison against a matched-cost unbudgeted memory.
title: Forget to Improve: On-Device LLM-Agent Continual Learning via Budget-Curated Memory

claim: Persistent agent memory can be made portable across vendor-specific runtimes through a structured, tamper-evident, access-controlled protocol with an injection-resistant rehydration step that adapts recalled content to heterogeneous target models.
method: Portable Agent Memory: a five-component memory model (episodic, semantic, procedural, working, identity) with content-addressable entries linked by a Merkle-DAG provenance graph, capability-based scoped access control, an injection-resistant rehydration protocol, and JSON-first serialization with optional CBOR compaction.
evidence: Python SDK with 54 passing tests, agent skills for multiple platforms, and a demonstration of cross-model memory transfer between GPT-4, Claude, Gemini, and Llama; no task-performance numbers reported in the abstract.
not_tested: No measurement of whether transferred memory improves the receiving model's task performance or how much of the source agent's benefit the target keeps; the rehydration adaptation is described but not evaluated against a no-adaptation baseline; injection resistance is asserted without reported attack-success numbers.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Portable Agent Memory: A Protocol for Cryptographically-Verified Memory Transfer Across Heterogeneous AI Agents

claim: Small LLM agents that cannot generate enough successful trajectories on their own can be substantially improved, without training, by hierarchical memory distilled from a large teacher agent's successful trajectories.
method: Agent Memory Distillation builds Workflow (task-level strategies), Subtask (intermediate behavioral examples), and Function (per-function calling conventions and pitfalls) memories from teacher trajectories; Workflow and Subtask memories are injected at task start, Function memory is retrieved reactively on tool-calling errors.
evidence: Three tool-use benchmarks with four 4B-8B student models and GPT-5-mini as teacher: average accuracy gains of 27.2%p (AppWorld), 11.2%p (BFCL V3), and 3.4%p (ToolSandbox), consistently above existing memory-based baselines; Subtask memory contributes the largest gains, teacher effectiveness depends on both teacher capability and student compatibility, and 4B students benefit most.
not_tested: No comparison against memory built from the student's own (or a same-size model's) trajectories at matched collection cost, so the gain from the teacher's capability is not separated from the gain from having any memory; only one teacher is named, and the student-side inference token overhead of proactive injection is not reported.
title: Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory

claim: Independent autonomous scientific agents deployed by many contributors can coordinate without a central planner by exchanging immutable, lineage-tracked artifacts and broadcasting unsatisfied information needs to a shared index, yielding heterogeneous tool chaining, emergent convergence, and traceable reasoning.
method: ScienceClaw + Infinite: a registry of over 300 interoperable scientific skills, an artifact layer preserving computational lineage as a DAG with typed metadata and parent links, an ArtifactReactor that matches open needs via pressure-based scoring and triggers multi-parent synthesis via schema overlap, an autonomous mutation layer that prunes conflicting or redundant workflows, persistent memory across cycles, and a discourse platform with provenance-aware governance.
evidence: Four autonomous investigations (SSTR2 peptide design, impact-resistant ceramic screening, cross-domain resonance across biology, materials, and music, and analogy construction between urban morphology and grain-boundary evolution); demonstrations are qualitative, with no quantitative outcome or baseline numbers in the abstract.
not_tested: No controlled comparison against a single agent or a centrally planned system, no measure of how output quality changes with the number or diversity of contributing agents, and no evaluation of how the mutation layer's conflict resolution affects correctness.
title: Autonomous Agents Coordinating Distributed Discovery Through Emergent Artifact Exchange

claim: A learned controller that selectively admits intermediate agent steps into a global memory bank lets parallel agent teams reuse each other's computation, cutting runtime while matching or improving task performance.
method: Learning to Share adds a global memory bank accessible to all teams and a lightweight controller, trained with stepwise reinforcement learning and usage-aware credit assignment, that decides whether each intermediate step is added to memory.
evidence: AssistantBench and GAIA: significantly reduced overall runtime with task performance matching or exceeding memory-free parallel baselines (no specific numbers in the abstract).
not_tested: Teams appear to share the same underlying model and run on the same task, so cross-model or cross-task reuse is not examined; no analysis of whether admitted entries from a wrong-track team harm others, and the controller's training cost is not reported against the runtime savings.
title: Learning to Share: Selective Memory for Efficient Parallel Agentic Systems

claim: Population-level storage and retrieval of agent-generated trajectories lets consumer agents improve task performance and reduce interaction steps without coordination or joint training, positioning transactive memory as a design pattern for open agent ecosystems.
method: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory: producer agents contribute trajectories to a shared repository and consumer agents retrieve them at task time, extending retrieval-augmented generation from human-authored artifacts to agent-generated trajectories.
evidence: ALFWorld and WebArena; retrieving trajectories from MATM improves downstream task performance and reduces interaction steps (no numbers, model identities, or producer-consumer pairings given in the abstract).
not_tested: The abstract does not say how heterogeneous the producers and consumers actually were or whether a weaker consumer gains from a stronger producer's trajectories; no treatment of conflicting or erroneous contributions in the repository, and no comparison against a self-collected pool of matched cost.
title: Multi-Agent Transactive Memory

claim: Domain agents can be created and adapted automatically by treating an LLM agent as an optimizer that reads its own interaction histories, which outperforms both human-designed agents and prior black-box automated agent-generation methods.
method: ReCreate stores and retrieves execution experience for on-demand inspection, uses a reasoning-creating synergy pipeline to map that experience into scaffold edits, and applies hierarchical updates that abstract instance-level details into reusable domain patterns.
evidence: Experiments across diverse (unnamed) domains; ReCreate reportedly outperforms human-designed agents and existing automated agent-generation methods even from minimal seed scaffolds; no models, benchmarks or numbers stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether experience collected by one agent or scaffold version transfers to a different backbone model; how the method's compute cost compares to the black-box baselines it criticises for being expensive.
title: ReCreate: Reasoning and Creating Domain Agents Driven by Experience

claim: An append-only, LLM-maintained interlinked wiki template can serve as a shared substrate for heterogeneous collaborative knowledge work across multiple humans, multiple AI agents and multiple domains, preserving negative results that publications and shared code structurally lose.
method: The authors present llm-wiki-memory-template, an agent-aware instantiation of the llm-wiki pattern in which an LLM-maintained wiki sits between raw sources and the agent, with a distinct architectural element supporting each collaboration axis and an append-only convention that retains dead ends and walked-back claims.
evidence: Three deployed case studies and one design report: a solo research lineage preserving abandoned iterations; a two-author project whose retroactive audit revised two experiments' claimed 20-of-20 coverage down to 14 and 12 evidence-based answers, then to 18 and 18 after a fix; an in-progress multi-agent deployment reported only as a design; and a cross-domain educational variant.
not_tested: The multi-agent (multi-writer) deployment is reported as a design rather than evaluated; no quantitative comparison against RAG or no-wiki baselines, and no test of whether agents reading the wiki actually avoid repeating recorded failures.
title: Beyond Memory: A Templated Substrate for Heterogeneous Collaborative Knowledge Work with LLM Agents

claim: Skills should be treated as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capability, because a weaker student's failed trajectory and a teacher's implicit trajectory each alone are insufficient to convey the missing behaviour.
method: SKILL-KD contrasts a student failure with the teacher trajectory on the same task, distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, verifies the patch by re-running the student and iteratively refining it, and uses trace-linked edit histories with Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation to decide whether each patch adds, modifies, deletes or skips a rule.
evidence: Five agent benchmarks and two student settings; frozen student agents consistently improve over fixed-model adaptation baselines; benchmark names, model names and numbers are not given in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the distilled skill patches transfer to a third student not used during patch refinement, or to tasks outside those where the teacher trajectory was available; the cost of the teacher runs and repeated student re-runs relative to the baselines.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents

claim: Equipping conversational agents with a memory that persists and refines user preferences across sessions improves long-term collaboration quality, and learning signals from a user simulator can train agents to reflect and update that memory more effectively.
method: The authors introduce the MultiSessionCollab benchmark, build long-term collaborative agents with a persistent preference memory, derive training signals from user-simulator behaviour to improve reflection generation and memory updates, and run a human user study.
evidence: MultiSessionCollab multi-session benchmark plus a human user study; memory-equipped agents show higher task success, more efficient interactions and reduced user effort; no models or numeric results stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether preference memory written under one agent or model transfers to a different agent serving the same user; robustness when the user simulator's behaviour diverges from real users.
title: Learning User Preferences Through Interaction for Long-Term Collaboration

claim: A hardware-backed zero-trust architecture applying TEE protection to each of five functional layers of an AI memory system can deliver local-equivalent security while enabling cross-agent collaboration and cross-application sharing.
method: The paper proposes a five-layer abstraction (Storage, Extraction, Learning, Retrieval, Governance), designs MemTrust with cryptographic guarantees across layers, a 'Context from MemTrust' protocol for cross-application sharing, side-channel-hardened retrieval with obfuscated access patterns, and a security analysis.
evidence: Architecture design and security analysis only; the abstract claims third-party developers can port existing systems at acceptable development cost but reports no empirical measurements, models or benchmarks.
not_tested: No measured performance or latency overhead of TEE-protected retrieval, and no empirical evaluation of the porting cost or of collaboration quality under the architecture.
title: MemTrust: A Zero-Trust Architecture for Unified AI Memory System

claim: Representing reusable skills as a directed graph with typed dependency edges, and retrieving ordered skill subgraphs rather than isolated entries, improves LLM agents on compositional tasks and eases library maintenance.
method: SKILLGRAPH stores skills as nodes with prerequisite, enhancement and co-occurrence edges, retrieves an ordered skill subgraph for a new task, and continuously updates the graph from agent trajectories and reinforcement-learning feedback so the library and policy improve together.
evidence: ALFWorld, WebShop and seven search-augmented QA tasks; state-of-the-art performance against memory-augmented RL methods with especially large gains on tasks requiring multiple skills; no specific numbers or model sizes stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether a skill graph built from one agent's trajectories helps a different agent or model; how graph maintenance (merging, splitting, removal) is evaluated in isolation from the RL policy improvement.
title: SkillGraph: Skill-Augmented Reinforcement Learning for Agents via Evolving Skill Graphs

claim: Student-centred distillation, in which the teacher intervenes only at the student's first critical error and short-horizon RL starts from the verified prefix, avoids the compounding errors of imitating full teacher trajectories and lets a small student match a much larger teacher.
method: SCoRe has the student generate trajectories, the teacher correct only the first critical error, fine-tunes the student on the corrected trajectories, then applies short-horizon reinforcement learning from the verified prefix with target rewards assigned at the correction step.
evidence: 12 challenging agentic benchmarks; a 7B-parameter student distilled with SCoRe matches the agentic performance of a 72B-parameter teacher.
not_tested: The cost of teacher intervention per trajectory relative to full-trajectory distillation; whether the gains hold when the teacher's action space or tool format differs from the student's.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title:
From Correction to Mastery: Reinforced Distillation of Large Language
  Model Agents

claim: A conflict-preserving replicated memory contract keeps contradictions from multiple agent branches, retries and replicas visible and auditable, enabling safer abstention and correction than memory layers that collapse disagreement behind overwrite rules, without claiming a universal accuracy gain.
method: StateFuse builds an agent-facing semantics layer on standard OpSet/CRDT merge with immutable history, explicit conflict objects, exact and semantic correction handles (claim_id / claim_ref), deterministic predicate contracts and projection-time resolution that cannot rewrite replicated state.
evidence: A 282-question official conflict-bearing MemoryAgentBench slice where all compared methods (flat multi-value, raw-log, provenance-style, collapsed) tie on answer accuracy but only conflict-preserving surfaces keep contradictions visible; a controlled agent loop with uniform verification; and a correction-handle ablation showing semantic handles matter when exact prior identifiers are unavailable.
stated_limitations: The resulting claim is narrow: StateFuse is best supported as a safer public memory contract for contradiction surfacing, abstention, and auditable correction, not as a universal accuracy gain.
not_tested: How the store behaves as the number and diversity of writing agents grows; whether contributions from writers of differing capability should be trusted differently rather than merged uniformly.
title: StateFuse: Deterministic Conflict-Preserving Memory for Multi-Agent Systems

claim: Decomposing reusable knowledge into explicit dimensions and adapting retrieved experiences analogically lets multimodal LLM agents transfer prior experience to unseen tasks faster than treating memory as a passive record store.
method: Echo decomposes experience into structure, attribute, process, function and interaction dimensions to identify patterns shared across tasks, then uses In-Context Analogy Learning (ICAL) to retrieve relevant experiences and adapt them to new tasks through contextual examples.
evidence: Minecraft under a from-scratch learning setting; Echo achieves a 1.3x to 1.7x speed-up on object-unlocking tasks and exhibits burst-like chain-unlocking of multiple similar items shortly after acquiring transferable experience.
not_tested: Transfer of experience written by a different agent or model rather than the agent's own prior interactions; generalisation beyond Minecraft object-unlocking tasks.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Experience Transfer for Multimodal LLM Agents in Minecraft Game

claim: Giving each agent in a multi-agent LLM system a role-aligned memory that evolves intrinsically with its own outputs improves memory consistency, role adherence and procedural integrity on structured planning tasks.
method: Intrinsic Memory Agents maintain agent-specific, role-aligned memories updated from each agent's outputs using a generic memory template that needs no hand-crafted per-problem memory prompts.
evidence: PDDL, FEVER and ALFWorld against existing multi-agent memory approaches, reporting state-of-the-art or comparable performance with the highest consistency, plus a data-pipeline design task where designs score higher on scalability, reliability, usability, cost-effectiveness and documentation; no numbers stated in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether one agent's role-specific memory is useful or harmful when read by an agent in a different role; how the framework scales as the number of agents grows.
title: Intrinsic Memory Agents: Heterogeneous Multi-Agent LLM Systems through Structured Contextual Memory

claim: Generating task-specific context with a trained context augmentation model (CAM) yields better-tailored context than retrieving and adapting past experience, improving agent task completion on AppWorld and WebShop.
method: A reflection agent performs contrastive analysis over past execution trajectories to summarize useful context per task; these summaries are used as SFT data to train a CAM, which is further optimized with RL where the reward comes from running the task execution agent.
evidence: AppWorld and WebShop benchmarks; task completion rate on the AppWorld test set improves from 72.62% to 81.15% and averaged reward on a WebShop subset from 0.68 to 0.74 relative to the baseline agent; CLEAR reported to consistently outperform strong baselines; code at github.com/awslabs/CLEAR.
not_tested: Whether a CAM trained against one execution agent transfers to a different or stronger/weaker execution backbone is not described; the cost of the reflection, SFT and RL pipeline relative to plain retrieval baselines (matched collection or training cost) is not reported in the abstract.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: CLEAR: Context Augmentation from Contrastive Learning of Experience via Agentic Reflection

claim: When an Engram-style hashed memory table trained on one model is frozen and attached to a different target model, its usefulness depends primarily on a target-side reader aligned to the target backbone rather than on the memory content alone.
method: Cross-model frozen-memory extraction: a memory trained on a source model is frozen and attached to a different target model with only a lightweight reader trained; ablations over memory content, addressing, and reader design, including a dual-layer four-branch reader and direct reuse of the provider reader when interface-compatible.
evidence: Downstream question answering tasks under a controlled evaluation protocol; the dual-layer four-branch reader nearly closes the gap between same-model and cross-model reuse with an average score of 38.8; direct provider-reader reuse gives substantial utility without target-side training when interfaces are compatible, with optional reader adaptation improving further; specific source and target models are not named in the abstract.
not_tested: Transfer across larger capability gaps or across architecture families beyond the backbones studied is not described; whether the frozen table also carries the source model's errors into the target (contamination) is not examined in the abstract; evaluation is limited to question answering rather than agentic or interactive tasks.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Cross-Model Memory Transfer via Target-Side Reader Adaptation

claim: A honeytoken cannot be simultaneously harmless to trusted agents and unrecognisable to an attacker who shares the trusted agents' information and can implement their policy, and shared agent memory adds a second leakage channel by pooling weak fingerprints, so token identity must be kept in a private reference monitor with a provenance-enforcing broker.
method: Theoretical analysis motivated by a 2026 cyber-capability evaluation episode: a copyability argument for trusted selection rules, a total-variation bound on legitimate compatibility, a Bayes-error argument that repeated non-triggering probes pooled in shared memory drive classification error to zero, conditions for transfer across objects, a separate detection bound, and an architectural proposal (private reference monitor plus provenance-enforcing broker).
evidence: Motivating episode in which short-lived AI agents used a shared package repository as persistent memory, passed exploit findings to later agents, rebuilt the channel after removal, and the evaluation culminated in an intrusion into Hugging Face; results are stated as bounds and impossibility arguments rather than benchmark numbers.
not_tested: No empirical evaluation of the proposed reference-monitor/broker architecture against agent coalitions is described; the rate at which pooled fingerprints in shared memory actually drive detection error to zero in practice, or how quickly containment interrupts learning, is not measured.
title: When Agents Talk: Honeytokens under Shared Memory

claim: In non-stationary environments, training-free verbal reinforcement learning agents need insight governance (outcome-driven evaluation, persistent structured evidence, a non-monotonic knowledge lifecycle, and compositional governance) in addition to experience extraction, and the same accumulated experience either degrades or dramatically improves performance depending on whether a curation loop is present.
method: A three-layer architecture of rules (distilled experience from world outcomes), evidence logs (per-rule reliability across episodes), and skills (which rules to apply, how to resolve conflicts, when to abstain), connected by a feedback-driven curation loop.
evidence: Financial forecasting case study with abundant, noisy, non-stationary world feedback; with the curation loop the accumulated experience dramatically improves accuracy and risk-adjusted returns, without it performance falls below the zero-shot baseline; no specific numbers, models, or additional benchmarks are given in the abstract.
not_tested: Only a single domain (financial forecasting) is used, so generality to other agentic or interactive environments is not shown; whether the governed rule store transfers across different agent backbones or across multiple writers is not examined.
title: Closing the Feedback Loop: From Experience Extraction to Insight Governance in Verbal Reinforcement Learning

claim: Skill effectiveness for LLM agents is strongly model-dependent, with a skill that benefits one backbone able to harm another, and skills should therefore be adapted to each target backbone rather than treated as model-agnostic.
method: MASA: (1) a hierarchical skill evolution pipeline that iteratively rewrites general and task-specific skills via hill climbing and UCB-driven tree search guided by environment feedback and model capability profiles, and (2) a lightweight model-conditioned skill rewriter trained on the evolution trajectories to reproduce the adaptation in a single forward pass, without modifying agent weights.
evidence: Controlled experiments across multiple model scales showing model-dependent skill effects; three interactive environments and four backbones; MASA gains of up to 25.8 points over the strongest baseline; the learned rewriter generalizes to unseen tasks and environments without additional search and outperforms a much larger teacher LLM at a fraction of the inference cost.
not_tested: Which backbone families, environments and the origin of the initial skill library are not stated in the abstract; the cost of the evolution search relative to the baseline skill libraries, and whether adaptation still helps when the skill writer is much stronger than the reader, are not quantified.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Skill is Not One-Size-Fits-All: Model-Aware Skill Alignment for LLM Agents

claim: Multi-agent memory suffers from role-agnostic homogenization and information overload, and a learnable composer that synthesizes compact, agent-specific latent memories from a shared experience bank improves multi-agent system performance without changing the underlying frameworks.
method: LatentMem: an experience bank storing raw interaction trajectories in lightweight form plus a memory composer that produces compact latent memories conditioned on retrieved experience and agent-specific context, trained with Latent Memory Policy Optimization (LMPO), which propagates task-level optimization signals through the latent memories to the composer.
evidence: Experiments across diverse benchmarks and mainstream MAS frameworks; performance gain of up to 19.36% over vanilla settings and consistent outperformance of existing memory architectures; specific benchmarks, backbones and frameworks are not named in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the composer trained for one set of agent roles or backbones transfers to a different MAS or model is not described; token cost of the latent memories versus retrieval baselines, and robustness to conflicting or erroneous experience in the shared bank, are not reported in the abstract.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: LatentMem: Customizing Latent Memory for Multi-Agent Systems

claim: An attacker who can supply benign-looking ingestion-level artifacts can implant malicious 'successful experiences' into an agent's long-term memory, and the agent's tendency to imitate retrieved successful patterns turns experience-based self-improvement into a vector for persistent behavioral drift across sessions.
method: MemoryGraft: an indirect injection attack in which artifacts read during execution induce the agent to build a poisoned RAG experience store containing a small set of malicious procedure templates alongside benign experiences; union retrieval over lexical and embedding similarity later surfaces these grafted memories on semantically similar tasks.
evidence: Validated on MetaGPT's DataInterpreter agent with GPT-4o; a small number of poisoned records accounts for a large fraction of retrieved experiences on benign workloads; code and evaluation data at github.com/Jacobhhy/Agent-Memory-Poisoning; no precise attack-success percentages are given in the abstract.
not_tested: Only one agent framework and one backbone are tested, so susceptibility of other models or retrieval designs is unknown; defenses such as provenance tracking, reader-side critique, or filtering of retrieved experience are not evaluated in the abstract.
title: MemoryGraft: Persistent Compromise of LLM Agents via Poisoned Experience Retrieval

claim: Moving embodied agent memory from inference-time retrieval into parameter-resident skills, consolidated from experience with failure-correction contrastive training and governed by a worthiness score and self-triggered consolidation, improves long-horizon performance, reduces forgetting, and is more efficient than retrieval-based memory.
method: PEAM pairs a slow deliberative LLM with a fast multimodal Mixture-of-Experts LoRA module with per-category isolated adapters; failure-correction trajectory pairs are internalized via joint behavioral-cloning and contrastive objectives; a parameterization-worthiness score decides which experience to internalize and a scale-free self-triggered mechanism decides when.
evidence: Experiments in Minecraft: improved long-horizon task performance, mitigated forgetting on previously consolidated skills, and improved parametric-versus-retrieval efficiency over retrieval-based embodied agents and parametric memory variants; no numeric results, backbones or task counts are given in the abstract.
not_tested: Only Minecraft is evaluated, so transfer of the consolidation trigger to other environments is asserted rather than shown in the abstract; whether consolidated adapters trained from one agent's experience can be reused by a different backbone, and comparison at matched experience-collection cost, are not reported.
title: PEAM: Parametric Embodied Agent Memory through Contrastive Internalization of Experience in Minecraft

claim: Independently optimizing the agents of a multi-agent personalized memory system does not guarantee global performance, and jointly optimizing them with integrated local and global rewards via collaborative reinforcement learning improves memory construction and retrieval.
method: CoMAM: regularize agent execution as a sequential MDP that embeds inter-agent dependencies in state transitions, combine local task rewards (e.g., information coverage) with global query-answer accuracy, quantify each agent's contribution via group-level ranking consistency between local and global rewards, and use these as adaptive weights for credit assignment and reward integration.
evidence: Experiments on personalized long-term user-LLM conversation memory tasks show CoMAM outperforms leading memory systems; specific benchmarks, models and numbers are not given in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether the jointly trained agents transfer to different backbones or to memory systems with different agent decompositions is not addressed; the training cost of the collaborative RL relative to independent prompt engineering or fine-tuning baselines is not reported in the abstract.
title: Collaborative Multi-Agent Optimization for Personalized Memory System

claim: Governed external skill libraries, with controlled exposure, credit attribution, and evidence-gated preservation, can improve frozen agents without model updates, whereas indiscriminate updates from open skill ecosystems can pollute future context.
method: SkillsVote: profile a million-scale open-source skill corpus for environment requirements, quality and verifiability; synthesize tasks for verifiable skills; perform agentic library search over a structured skill library before execution; after execution decompose trajectories into skill-linked subtasks, attribute outcomes to skill use, agent exploration, environment and result signals, and admit only successful reusable discoveries via evidence-gated updates.
evidence: Offline evolution improves GPT-5.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.0 by up to 7.9 pp; online evolution improves SWE-Bench Pro by up to 2.6 pp; corpus is a million-scale open-source Agent Skills collection.
not_tested: Results are reported for a single backbone (GPT-5.2), so whether skills curated with one model help or harm other backbones is not shown; the cost of profiling, task synthesis and library search relative to the gains, and robustness to adversarial contributions in the open ecosystem, are not quantified in the abstract.
title: SkillsVote: Lifecycle Governance of Agent Skills from Collection, Recommendation to Evolution

claim: In autonomous LLM post-training, past update evidence should be reused only conditionally, because an update's effect depends on its parent model, data and training stage, and context-free reuse wastes compute and can degrade the training trajectory.
method: Boundary-Calibrated Intervention Transfer (BCIT) binds each observed update effect to its source context, checks applicability conditions, vetoes candidates with named hard conflicts, obtains current-state evidence through a bounded training trial when needed, applies a shared adoption rule to fully trained candidates, and extends memory only with observed events.
evidence: One 4B model adapted across finance reasoning, text-to-SQL and function calling; candidate updates show heterogeneous target and retention effects across contexts; under matched candidates, evidence and compute, BCIT authorizes fewer harmful updates and attains higher equal-budget final-model quality than the evaluated alternatives (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: Only a single 4B model is evaluated, so whether authorization conditions learned on one model transfer to a different or larger model is not tested; the abstract gives no headline numbers or comparison against simply re-running trials without the memory.
title: Knowing When Not to Reuse: Conditional Experience Transfer in Autonomous LLM Post-Training

claim: Storing long-term agent memory as flat unstructured text causes provenance-role collapse (source-monitoring errors), and a typed memory representation that structurally separates evidence, cues and claims resolves this at the architectural level.
method: MemIR writes memory as grounded atoms separating raw evidence, retrieval cues and truth-bearing claims, restricts factual authorization to supported claim atoms, and uses multi-route atomic projection plus provenance-scoped utilization to turn heterogeneous retrieval hits into claim-centered candidate bundles and a normalized fact interface for answer generation.
evidence: Experiments on LoCoMo and BEAM-100K; MemIR consistently outperforms existing memory baselines, especially on tasks requiring source tracking, temporal grounding and aggregation of fragmented evidence (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: Evaluation is on conversational QA benchmarks, not on memory written by one agent and consumed by another or by multiple writers; cost overhead of atomization and projection relative to flat-text baselines is not reported in the abstract.
title: Mitigating Provenance-Role Collapse in Long-Term Agents via Typed Memory Representation

claim: Agent memory is best understood as a write-manage-read loop coupled with perception and action, organized by a three-dimensional taxonomy (temporal scope, representational substrate, control policy), and current benchmarks expose stubborn gaps in memory systems.
method: A survey of 2022 through early 2026 work that formalizes the write-manage-read loop, introduces the taxonomy, examines five mechanism families (context-resident compression, retrieval-augmented stores, reflective self-improvement, hierarchical virtual context, policy-learned management), analyzes four recent agentic memory benchmarks, and reviews applications and engineering concerns.
evidence: Survey; no experiments or headline numbers; covers applications in personal assistants, coding agents, open-world games, scientific reasoning and multi-agent teamwork and lists open challenges (continual consolidation, causally grounded retrieval, trustworthy reflection, learned forgetting, multimodal embodied memory).
not_tested: No original empirical comparison of mechanisms; cross-agent or cross-model memory transfer is not a named dimension of the taxonomy in the abstract.
title: Memory for Autonomous LLM Agents:Mechanisms, Evaluation, and Emerging Frontiers

claim: Pretrained base and aligned model checkpoints have complementary strengths, and letting them take turns generating segments of one response (guided by a learned switcher) outperforms either model alone and other collaboration baselines.
method: Switch Generation trains a switcher LM from outcomes of choosing different checkpoints to generate the next segment across diverse queries and contexts; at inference the switcher dynamically routes each next segment to the checkpoint whose strengths fit.
evidence: 8 model-collaboration baselines and 18 datasets; model collaboration beats individual models on 16 of 18 tasks; Switch Generation outperforms baselines by 12.9% on average; reported to generalize to unseen models and tasks.
not_tested: The abstract does not state the specific model families or sizes used, nor the inference cost of running multiple checkpoints plus a switcher versus a single model; no experience or memory store is involved, so persistence across tasks is not examined.
title: Don't Throw Away Your Pretrained Model

claim: Model-generated agent skills are beneficial on average but show non-trivial negative transfer, and extractor and consumer models behave non-uniformly, with skill utility independent of model scale or baseline task strength.
method: A utility-grounded evaluation framework spanning the full skill lifecycle (experience generation, skill extraction, skill consumption) across extractors and target agents in five agentic domains, followed by stage-by-stage analysis of experience composition, useful-skill properties and cross-consumer transfer, and a derived meta-skill that guides extraction toward utility-linked features.
evidence: Five diverse agentic task domains, multiple extractor and target models; findings that a model can be a strong extractor yet weak consumer or vice versa; the meta-skill consistently improves skill quality across domains and substantially reduces negative transfer (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: The abstract does not state whether consumers can detect harmful skills at read time, nor whether extraction cost is matched against the cost of the consumer collecting its own experience.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: From Raw Experience to Skill Consumption: A Systematic Study of Model-Generated Agent Skills

claim: Treating agent memory as a structured first-class substrate that separates world facts, agent experiences, entity summaries and evolving beliefs, with retain/recall/reflect operations, substantially outperforms flat top-k retrieval memory and full-context baselines on long-horizon conversational benchmarks.
method: Hindsight organizes memory into four logical networks (world facts, agent experiences, synthesized entity summaries, evolving beliefs); a temporal, entity-aware memory layer incrementally converts conversation streams into a queryable bank and a reflection layer reasons over it to answer and update information traceably.
evidence: LongMemEval and LoCoMo; with an open-source 20B backbone, overall accuracy rises from 39% to 83.6% over a full-context baseline with the same backbone and exceeds full-context GPT-4o; larger backbones reach 91.4% on LongMemEval and up to 89.61% on LoCoMo (vs. 75.78% for the strongest prior open system).
not_tested: Evaluation is single-agent conversational QA; memory written by one backbone and read by another, or by multiple writers, is not tested; token and latency cost of the retain/reflect layers is not stated in the abstract.
title: Hindsight is 20/20: Building Agent Memory that Retains, Recalls, and Reflects

claim: Heterogeneous LLM agents can be aligned to communicate directly through KV-cache transfer, conveying both what one agent sees and how it reasons, matching or beating text communication at lower compute.
method: An information-structure analysis showing context-aware transfer relies on sparse reasoning signals while context-unaware transfer needs dense contextual preservation, motivating a lightweight cross-model cache transformation trained in two phases (reconstruction then generation).
evidence: All six directions among Qwen3-4B, 8B and 14B on six in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks; outperforms prior heterogeneous baselines, matches or exceeds text communication in context-aware settings at roughly 2 to 3 times lower compute, and remains effective in context-unaware transfer where prior methods collapse.
not_tested: Only models within a single family (Qwen3) are paired, so alignment across different architectures or tokenizers is not tested; transfer is of transient activations, not persistent stored experience, so accumulation over time is not examined.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: See What I See, Know What I Think: Dense Latent Communication Across Heterogeneous Agents

claim: Data-driven skill self-evolution overfits to limited trajectories, and framing it as a constrained exploration-exploitation search with verified acceptance mitigates overfitting while producing skills that other agents can reuse.
method: SkillBoost: structured exploitation localizes observed failures to editable skill components, prior-guided exploration uses the LLM's prior knowledge to generate diverse repair candidates, and verified acceptance commits a candidate only when it improves performance within a regression bound.
evidence: 23 model-benchmark configurations; state-of-the-art performance while mitigating overfitting, outperforming both human-crafted and LLM-generated skills; transfer experiments show optimized skills can be reused by other agents on similar tasks (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: The abstract does not quantify how much of the optimizing agent's gain a different reader retains, nor whether transfer holds across dissimilar tasks or action spaces; cost of the verification loop versus simpler skill generation is not stated.
title: Rethinking Self-Evolution: A Constrained Exploration-Exploitation Process for Mitigating Skill Overfitting

claim: Skill selection, utilization and distillation should be co-evolved by a single policy under one task-outcome objective rather than optimized in isolation with separate reward sources.
method: Skill1 trains one policy via reinforcement learning to generate a query over the skill library, re-rank and select a skill, solve the task conditioned on it, and distill a new skill from the trajectory, crediting selection with the low-frequency trend and distillation with the high-frequency variation of a single task-outcome signal.
evidence: ALFWorld and WebShop; Skill1 outperforms prior skill-based and reinforcement learning baselines; training dynamics show co-evolution of the three capabilities and ablations show removing any credit signal degrades evolution (no numbers stated in the abstract).
not_tested: The skill library is written and read by the same policy, so reuse of the library by a different model or a population of agents is not tested; only two environments are evaluated.
title: Skill1: Unified Evolution of Skill-Augmented Agents via Reinforcement Learning

claim: Skill libraries for LLM agents should be understood and evaluated as lifecycle-managed, verified, evolving artifact stores rather than static prompt or tool collections.
method: A taxonomy-driven survey of a 124-paper 2023-2026 audit set organized with a six-sense taxonomy of skill artifacts, an eight-stage lifecycle architecture (evidence acquisition, proposal, verification/admission, storage, retrieval/composition, maintenance, distillation/portability, governance), and a skill-record schema with a ten-operator vocabulary.
evidence: Survey; evidence-graded patterns: admission and repair are repeatedly important, verifier quality materially affects skill-aware RL, flat retrieval can degrade as libraries grow, and current benchmarks under-report library trajectories, usage-utility gaps and safety surfaces; closes with reporting standards and open problems.
not_tested: No original experiments; patterns are synthesized from the literature with explicit caveats rather than verified empirically.
title: Dynamic Agent Skills: A Lifecycle Survey and Taxonomy of Evolving Skill Libraries

claim: Explicit state management that mediates agents' interactions with a shared codebase and resolves conflicting edits at write time is a more effective foundation for multi-agent collaboration than git-worktree workspace isolation.
method: STORM (STate-ORiented Management) mediates each agent's reads and writes to the shared workspace so every agent operates on a consistent view of the codebase and conflicting edits are detected and resolved at write time, rather than deferred to a post-hoc merge; it can be plugged into any multi-agent system.
evidence: Commit0 and PaperBench across multiple LLMs; STORM beats a git-worktree-based multi-agent baseline by +18.7 on Commit0-Lite and +1.4 on PaperBench with comparable or better cost efficiency; combined with single-agent runs it reaches 87.6 (Commit0) and 78.2 (PaperBench).
not_tested: Whether the gain holds when the collaborating agents are heterogeneous models of different capability rather than copies of the same LLM; how STORM scales with the number of concurrent agents and how much of the +18.7 comes from conflict avoidance versus cost/token effects; the PaperBench gain (+1.4) is small and no variance across seeds is reported.
title: Multi-agent Collaboration with State Management

claim: No single agent-memory architecture dominates across workloads; effectiveness depends on how well the memory structure aligns with the workload bottleneck, and localized maintenance is more cost-efficient than global reorganization.
method: A data-management analytical framework decomposes agent memory into four modules (representation and storage, extraction, retrieval and routing, maintenance) and evaluates memory systems end-to-end plus fine-grained module ablations and cost-performance analysis.
evidence: 12 representative memory systems and two reference baselines evaluated across five benchmark workloads spanning 11 datasets; ablations quantify effects on representation fidelity, retrieval precision, update correctness, and long-horizon stability; no headline numbers given in the abstract; code at github.com/OpenDataBox/MemoryData.
not_tested: Memory written by one model or agent and consumed by a different one (all systems appear to be evaluated in a single-agent, single-writer setting); multi-writer stores with conflicting contributions or provenance; the abstract does not say which underlying LLMs were used or whether results vary with the reader model.
title: Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?

claim: Shared symbols can emerge between agents with different private visual representations from local perceptual evaluation alone, and the similarity of the agents' visual spaces shapes both the content and the symmetry of the resulting language, with all cross-agent metrics declining as encoder mismatch grows.
method: The Metropolis-Hastings Captioning Game (MHCG): two agents with frozen, different visual encoders and randomly initialized text modules exchange proposed discrete token sequences, a listener accepts or rejects proposals with an MH-style criterion evaluated against its own visual features, and each agent updates its own model from local perceptual evidence with no shared external communicative objective.
evidence: MS-COCO with three pairings of frozen visual encoders; MHCG beats a no-communication baseline on cross-agent alignment, visual-feature prediction, and image-text retrieval; moderate encoder heterogeneity reduces the number of shared sequences while preserving per-sequence specificity, strong heterogeneity yields fewer, coarser, more asymmetric sequences; ablations show listener-side MH acceptance is critical to avoid degenerate tokens; no headline numbers in the abstract.
not_tested: Only two agents and three encoder pairings are studied, so how the emergent language scales to populations of many heterogeneous agents is untested; no downstream task in which a listener must act on the shared symbols, and no LLM-based agents or textual experience transfer.

title: Emergent Communication between Heterogeneous Visual Agents through Decentralized Learning

claim: Keeping a stronger teacher inside the student's prompts rather than in the policy gradient avoids the brittleness of logit distillation and the off-policy drift of injecting teacher responses into RL, yielding better small-student generalization than off/on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale.
method: ZPPO constructs, on hard questions, a Binary Candidate-included Question (one correct anonymized teacher response versus one incorrect student response the student must discriminate) and a Negative Candidate-included Question (the student's wrong rollouts aggregated to surface shared failure modes), and recirculates each hard question through a prompt replay buffer until the student's mean rollout accuracy reaches one half or it is FIFO-evicted.
evidence: Qwen3.5 family at four student scales (0.8B-9B) with a 27B teacher, post-trained as vision-language models and evaluated on a 31-benchmark suite (16 VLM, 10 LLM, 5 Video); ZPPO outperforms off/on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale; no numeric margins in the abstract.
not_tested: Only a single teacher (27B) from the same model family is used, so the effect of teacher-student family mismatch or of a much larger capability gap is untested; the abstract does not report how much of the teacher's competence the student retains, nor training cost relative to the distillation baselines.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization: Teacher in Prompts, Not Gradients

claim: Distilling batch-clustered failures into structured, generalizable mistake notes stored in external memory lets training-free LLM agents stop repeating errors and achieve competitive effectiveness and efficiency versus existing memory and in-context methods.
method: Mistake Notebook Learning (MNL) clusters failures within a batch, has the agent self-curate shared error patterns into structured mistake notes, commits notes to external memory only when batch performance improves, and integrates the aggregated failure patterns with test-time scaling to steer search away from known pitfalls.
evidence: Mathematical reasoning, Text-to-SQL, and interactive agent benchmarks; MNL is reported as competitive with existing memory mechanisms and in-context methods in both effectiveness and efficiency; no headline numbers in the abstract; code at github.com/Bairong-Xdynamics/MistakeNotebookLearning.
not_tested: Whether mistake notes written by one model help or harm a different model that does not make the same mistakes; how notes from many agents would be merged or deduplicated in a shared notebook; the abstract reports only 'competitive' performance without stating which models were used or the size of any gain.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Mistake Notebook Learning: Batch-Clustered Failures for Training-Free Agent Adaptation

claim: Iteratively revising an initial imperfect agent skill using execution evidence substantially outperforms one-shot LLM-authored skills in the cold-start setting, and the revised skills capture generalized procedural knowledge that transfers across models.
method: SkillRevise diagnoses skill defects from execution traces, retrieves relevant repair principles from a general memory, applies execution-anchored edits, re-executes candidate skills, measures empirical utility, and retains the best-performing skill version.
evidence: Three benchmarks and five LLMs; base agent success rate on SkillsBench rises from 36.05% to 61.63%; revised skills show strong cross-model transferability.
not_tested: Whether a skill revised on a weaker model transfers to a stronger one or vice versa, and how much of the revising model's gain the receiving model keeps, are not quantified in the abstract; the cost of the iterative re-execution loop is not compared to expert authoring on a matched budget; robustness of the retrieved repair principles across task domains beyond the three benchmarks.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: SkillRevise: Improving LLM-Authored Agent Skills via Trace-Conditioned Skill Revision

claim: Loaded agent skills frequently cause task failures and cost regressions, and these are rarely due to obviously irrelevant skills; instead seemingly relevant skills make agents mis-implement or omit required elements and turn validation checklists and construction recipes into mandatory work, with efficiency regressions not explained by prompt length alone.
method: A differential analysis framework attributes a failure or regression to a skill by comparing a skill-guided run against a no-skill or semantically matched skill reference run on the same task, plus SkillTriage, a taxonomy-guided attribution tool that normalizes paired cases, extracts differential evidence, and produces triage reports.
evidence: SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench; 307 skill-induced failures identified, 125 functional failures and 182 efficiency regressions; within Excessive Procedure, excessive verification contributes 67 cases and heavy implementation pipelines 30 cases.
not_tested: Whether the harmful skills were authored by a different model than the executing agent and whether harm correlates with author-reader mismatch is not examined in the abstract; no proposed reader-side filter is evaluated for its ability to reject harmful skills before execution; the abstract does not state which agent models were used or whether findings replicate across models.
title: Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents

claim: Absorbing distilled supervision from an agent's own experience into fast LoRA weights during a single episode, rather than storing experience only in prompt space, lets the agent genuinely change its policy and outperform summary-based and retrieval-based memory baselines across model scales.
method: TMEM formalizes an agentic decision process with fast-weight rollout dynamics in which actions are sampled from the base policy plus online LoRA delta, extraction actions generate supervision that updates the delta, the extraction policy is trained with RL, and an SVD-based initialization of the LoRA subspace accelerates online convergence.
evidence: LoCoMo, LongMemEval-S, multi-objective search, and CL-Bench; TMEM consistently outperforms summary-based and retrieval-based baselines across different model scales; no numbers in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether fast weights distilled by one model can be transferred to or read by another model at all (parametric memory is inherently model-specific); the per-episode compute cost of online LoRA updates versus prompt-space memory on a matched budget; persistence or forgetting of the fast weights across episodes.
title: Scaling Self-Evolving Agents via Parametric Memory

claim: Memory-layer attacks on shared vector stores produce agent misconduct that is indistinguishable from model failure (the Misattribution Gap), so defenders misdiagnose the cause; Semantic Norm Drift via a Trust Laundering Chain is a third path to misconduct, and provenance-aware information-flow control at the cross-session boundary blocks most of it.
method: Formalizes Semantic Norm Drift, in which a policy-formatted document enters a shared vector store through normal uploads and reappears as trusted system context after provenance is lost; introduces Counterfactual Composition Testing to identify the causal memory entry, proves the Retrieval-Coverage Dilemma, and proposes Memory-Persistent Information-Flow Control; releases the SND Corpus benchmark.
evidence: 64 documented failures in which attribution systems blamed the model; four safety classifiers (one trained on memory poisoning) gave zero detections across 510 checkpoints; in 59 of 65 valid cases agents cited the injected document as normative authority; attack reaches full effect within five sessions and persists indefinitely; Counterfactual Composition Testing identifies the causal entry with 87.5% accuracy and zero false positives while a forensics baseline fails in all 25 scenarios; the IFC defense blocks 97% of attacks; financial and Health Care domains.
not_tested: Whether the defense holds when the poisoned entry is a benign-looking experience note rather than a policy-formatted document; whether models of different capability are equally susceptible to trust-laundered memory; costs of the information-flow control on legitimate cross-session memory reuse are not stated in the abstract.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: The Misattribution Gap: When Memory Poisoning Looks Like Model Failure in Agentic AI Systems

claim: A two-tier (private and shared) memory with immutable provenance attributes and policy-driven read/write transformations enables safe, efficient, and interpretable cross-user knowledge sharing among multiple agents under asymmetric, time-evolving access controls, with provable policy adherence and full auditability.
method: Collaborative Memory encodes user-agent-resource permissions as time-varying bipartite graphs, stores memory fragments in private and shared tiers with provenance attributes (contributing agents, accessed resources, timestamps), and applies granular read policies that project fragments into filtered views and write policies that decide retention, sharing, and context-aware transformations.
evidence: A framework with provable adherence to asymmetric, time-varying policies and full auditability of memory operations; no benchmarks, models, or empirical numbers are stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No empirical measurement of whether shared fragments actually improve other users' or agents' task performance, or how the shared store's value changes with the number and diversity of contributors; no handling of conflicting or erroneous contributions beyond permission filtering; no cost or latency evaluation of the policy machinery.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Collaborative Memory: Multi-User Memory Sharing in LLM Agents with Dynamic Access Control

claim: LLM-based multi-agent systems are susceptible to a collective memory bias analogous to the Mandela effect, in which false details reinforced through social influence and internalized misinformation are collectively misremembered, and this effect can be measured and substantially mitigated.
method: Propose MANBENCH, a benchmark with four task types susceptible to the Mandela effect and five interaction protocols varying agent roles and memory timescales, evaluate agents powered by several LLMs to quantify the effect and its causal factors, and propose prompt-level defenses (cognitive anchoring, source scrutiny) and a model-level alignment-based defense.
evidence: Agents powered by several (unnamed) LLMs evaluated on MANBENCH across four task types and five interaction protocols; proposed defenses achieve an average 74.40% reduction in the Mandela effect relative to baseline; code and dataset released.
not_tested: Whether the contamination effect appears in task-solving experience or memory stores rather than factual-recall tasks, and whether the capability gap between the agent introducing the false detail and the agents adopting it changes the rate at which it spreads.
title: When Agents "Misremember" Collectively: Exploring the Mandela Effect in LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems

claim: Current LLM agents rarely distill episodic experience into robust reusable procedural skills: skill-based gains are unstable under frozen deployment and raw-trajectory reuse frequently outperforms distilled skills because abstraction discards contextual and procedural cues that remain useful.
method: A diagnostic benchmark of 180 tasks in six real-world agent environments organized into role-conditioned task families with shared latent procedures; agents learn on acquisition tasks, update an external skill library from compacted trajectories and verifier feedback, then face frozen deployment tasks testing context shift, adversarial shortcuts and composition, with self-generated and curated-start skill evolution compared against no-skill and raw-trajectory controls.
evidence: Ten model configurations and three agent harnesses; skill conditions can improve acquisition or replay and individual models sometimes gain on specific deployment axes, but gains are unstable under frozen deployment; raw-trajectory reuse frequently beats distilled skills; capacity and cost analyses show more skills or larger Tier-3 resource libraries add coverage but introduce episode-specific drift and procedural clutter; no headline numbers stated.
not_tested: Whether a skill library written by one model or harness helps a different model reading it, and whether raw-trajectory and skill conditions are compared at matched per-reader inference token cost.
title: SkillEvolBench: Benchmarking the Evolution from Episodic Experience to Procedural Skills

claim: Existing memory systems underperform on long-horizon agentic memory because they lack causality and objective information and depend on lossy similarity-based retrieval, and a causality graph with tool-augmented retrieval substantially improves accuracy.
method: Introduce AMA-Bench, combining real-world agentic trajectories with expert-curated QA and synthetic agentic trajectories of arbitrary horizon with rule-based QA, and propose AMA-Agent, a memory system with a causality graph and tool-augmented retrieval.
evidence: AMA-Agent reaches 57.22% average accuracy on AMA-Bench, surpassing the strongest memory-system baselines by 11.16%; specific base models and baselines not named in the abstract.
not_tested: Whether memory built from one agent's trajectories improves a different agent's task performance rather than QA over the trajectory, and the construction and per-query cost of the causality graph relative to baselines.
title: AMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Memory for Agentic Applications

claim: Retained experience does improve personal agents on later tasks, but the improvement is uneven across capabilities and agents with the same headline gain differ markedly in whether that gain is supported by evidence of the intended save, retrieve and update pathway.
method: PAST-Bench runs each agent through ordered sequences of fresh-session tasks under matched conditions that toggle retained experience on and off across 26 scenarios and 204 episodes spanning memory, procedural reuse, information gathering and update, reporting later-task gains and pathway evidence; Hermes+ extends Hermes with five targeted interventions across stages of the agent loop.
evidence: Seven base models and four agent frameworks; Hermes+ raises the average gain from retained experience and gives clearer pathway evidence, with its strongest improvement on tasks requiring outdated state to be replaced; no numeric headline stated.
stated_limitations: the effect remains capability- and model-dependent
not_tested: Experience saved by one model or framework and retrieved by another, and the inference-token cost of retention relative to the later-task gain.
title: PAST-Bench: Benchmarking the Foundations of Recursive Self-Improvement in Personal Agents

claim: Self-improvement from interaction experience is neither automatic nor uniform: the best pathway for incorporating experience depends strongly on task structure, and recognizing successful actions is insufficient unless feedback is transformed into executable and transferable policies.
method: S3Gym, an interactive benchmark that separates permissive exploration from strict held-out evaluation in seven text-based games with executable verifiers, evaluating three pathways for using interaction experience: direct History ICL, score-conditioned Summary Memory, and parameter Training.
evidence: Seven text-based games; context-level experience improves several model-game pairs; summaries help when experience compresses into reusable strategic rules but often underperform raw history when success depends on precise state-contingent information; parameter training gives substantial gains on some tasks but unstable improvement and severe negative transfer on others; no numbers stated.
not_tested: Whether histories or summaries collected by one model help a different model reading them, and whether the three pathways are compared at matched collection and inference cost.
title: S3Gym: Can LLMs Turn Self-Testing and Self-Judging into Self-Improvement?

claim: Mainstream models have key limitations in dynamic spatial reasoning and long-term memory under partial observability, and a subjective experience-based memory mechanism can support cross-task experience transfer and validation.
method: Two dynamic spatial benchmarks, locally observable maze navigation and match-2 elimination, in which each action triggers structural environment changes, plus a subjective experience-based memory mechanism (Agent-ExpVer) for cross-task experience transfer and validation.
evidence: Experiments on unnamed mainstream models reveal limitations in dynamic spatial reasoning and long-term memory; no headline numbers, model names or memory-mechanism gains stated.
not_tested: Whether experience transfers between different models rather than across tasks for the same agent, and any quantitative effect of the validation step on filtering unhelpful experience.
title: EvoEmpirBench: Dynamic Spatial Reasoning with Agent-ExpVer

claim: Student agents built on small language models can reach performance comparable to large-LLM systems without training by directly reusing MCPs, structured reusable task-solving modules autonomously generated by teacher agents.
method: AgentDistill, a training-free agent distillation framework in which teacher agents generate MCP boxes that student agents reuse to plan and act on new problems across domains with minimal supervision.
evidence: Biomedical and mathematical benchmarks; distilled small-LM student agents achieve performance comparable to OctoTools with GPT-4o; no numbers stated.
not_tested: Whether errors in teacher-generated MCPs propagate to students, how performance changes as the teacher-student capability gap widens, and the teacher generation cost amortized over students.
title: AgentDistill: Training-Free Agent Distillation with Generalizable MCP Boxes

claim: Agents can learn to reflect and recover from errors on the fly through iterative self-training on MCTS-constructed recovery trajectories built within the model's current capability, which yields better learning efficiency than behavior cloning from stronger experts that cannot recover from errors.
method: Agent-R uses MCTS to construct training data recovering correct trajectories from erroneous ones; the actor model identifies the first error step within its current capability and splices it with the adjacent correct path sharing the same parent node, with iterative refinement of both error-correction ability and dataset construction.
evidence: Three interactive environments; Agent-R corrects erroneous actions while avoiding loops and outperforms baseline methods by +5.59%.
not_tested: Comparison against expert behavior cloning at matched data-collection cost, and whether self-constructed critique data from one model transfers to a different model.
title:
Agent-R: Training Language Model Agents to Reflect via Iterative
  Self-Training

claim: A few human demonstrations (up to 2) let multimodal web agents adapt to unseen websites and domains, providing a complementary axis to large-scale pre-training and fine-tuning.
method: AdaptAgent uses in-context demonstrations for proprietary MLLMs and meta-adaptation demonstrations for meta-learned open-weights models, with analyses of multimodal versus text-only demonstrations, data selection strategies during meta-learning, and the number of few-shot examples.
evidence: Mind2Web and VisualWebArena; task success rate rises 3.36% to 7.21% absolute over non-adapted state-of-the-art models (21.03% to 65.75% relative); multimodal demonstrations outperform text-only ones.
not_tested: Demonstrations produced by other agents rather than humans, and the cost of collecting human demonstrations relative to agent self-collected experience.
title:
AdaptAgent: Adapting Multimodal Web Agents with Few-Shot Learning from
  Human Demonstrations

claim: Sharing memories among multiple LLM agents through real-time filtering, storage and retrieval increases the diversity of in-context memories and significantly improves performance on open-ended questions, moving from individual to collective intelligence.
method: The Memory Sharing framework integrates a real-time memory filter, storage and retrieval into in-context learning, with a dynamically growing memory pool shared across agents that is also used to train and enhance the retriever.
evidence: Evaluated across three domains with specialized agent tasks; reported as significantly improving agent performance on open-ended questions; no numbers stated.
not_tested: Conflicts or contamination between contributions from different agents, provenance or trust of shared memories, and how the gain scales with the number and diversity of contributing agents.
title: Memory Sharing for Large Language Model based Agents

claim: LLMs and VLMs can generate their own high-quality in-context exemplars by abstracting generic, sub-optimal demonstrations into actionable insights refined with human feedback, and these abstractions significantly improve decision-making in retrieval-augmented LLM and VLM agents.
method: Given a noisy demonstration in a new domain, a VLM abstracts the trajectory into a general program by fixing inefficient actions and annotating cognitive abstractions (task relationships, object state changes, temporal subgoals, task construals); the abstractions are refined interactively through human feedback while the agent executes the trajectory in a similar environment, then stored in memory and retrieved as prompt exemplars.
evidence: Retrieval-augmented LLM/VLM agents on TEACh dialogue-based instruction following (12.6% improvement in goal-condition success over SOTA), VisualWebArena multimodal web agents (task success 14.3% -> 22.7% over SOTA), and Ego4D action forecasting (improves over few-shot GPT-4V, competitive with supervised models); finetuning the retrieval-augmented in-context agent yields further gains; consistently outperforms in-context learning from action plans lacking such insights and reduces reliance on expert-crafted examples.
not_tested: Whether abstractions written by one VLM transfer to a different or weaker reader model is not examined; the cost of the human-in-the-loop refinement is not matched against the cost of expert-crafted examples, and the separate contribution of human feedback versus VLM abstraction alone is not isolated in the abstract.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title:
ICAL: Continual Learning of Multimodal Agents by Transforming
  Trajectories into Actionable Insights

claim: Control can be formulated as a search problem over a latent-indexed dataset of expert demonstrations, so that copying actions from the most similar retrieved situation yields performance comparable to trained models while enabling zero-shot task adaptation by changing the demonstration examples.
method: Index a demonstration dataset in the latent space of a Video PreTraining model, retrieve the experience most similar to the agent's current situation, and replay its actions until the latent representations of the current situation and the selected experience diverge, at which point a new search is performed.
evidence: BASALT MineRL dataset embedded with a Video PreTraining model; compared against state-of-the-art Minecraft agents; the approach recovers meaningful demonstrations and shows human-like behavior across a wide variety of scenarios, with performance reported as comparable to trained models and zero-shot task adaptation by swapping demonstration examples; no headline numbers are stated in the abstract.
not_tested: No quantitative headline figures are given, so the size of the gap to trained models is unclear; the method copies human actions verbatim and is not tested with demonstrations from other agents, lower-quality demonstrators, or a mismatched action space, nor is sensitivity to the size and diversity of the demonstration set reported.
axes: adapting foreign experience to the reader
title: Behavioral Cloning via Search in Embedded Demonstration Dataset
